title: Aloo Gobi
subtitle: Indian potato and cauliflower curry
excerpt: Aloo gobi is a dry vegetable curry of potatoes and cauliflower cooked with warm spices until just tender. It is one of the most straightforward curries to make at home. The key is a medium heat and patience -- the vegetables should soften without going mushy.
sourceNotes: Aloo gobi is a North Indian staple, cooked in every Punjab household. The dry style -- without much sauce -- is the traditional home version. Restaurant versions often add tomato paste or cream to create a thicker gravy.

content.text: Keep the cauliflower florets and potato cubes roughly the same size so they cook evenly. The tomatoes are added in a small amount -- just enough to coat the vegetables without making a sauce.
Heat the oil in a wide pan over medium heat. Add the cumin seeds. When they sizzle and pop, add the onion.
Cook the onion for 8 minutes until golden. Add the garlic and ginger and cook for 2 minutes.
Add the turmeric and coriander. Stir for 1 minute. Add the tinned tomatoes and cook for 3 minutes until the mixture thickens.
Add the potato cubes and toss to coat in the spice paste. Pour in 100ml of water. Cover and cook on low heat for 10 minutes.
Add the cauliflower florets and stir gently. Add salt. Cover again and cook for another 12 minutes until both vegetables are just tender.
Remove the lid and cook for 2 minutes to drive off any remaining moisture. Sprinkle with garam masala. Taste and adjust seasoning. Serve as a side dish.

items.cause: It was added too early or cooked at too high a heat
items.fix: Add cauliflower only once the potatoes are half done, and keep the heat low
Add a small splash of water -- 2 tablespoons -- and stir gently to lift anything stuck to the base

items.cause: Insufficient salt or the spices were not fried long enough
items.fix: Taste carefully and add salt in small amounts; fry the ground spices for a full 60 seconds next time

content.text: Aloo gobi is eaten across North India and Pakistan. It is particularly popular in Punjab and Uttar Pradesh. In British Indian restaurants it has been on menus since the 1960s. At home it is made as a dry dish -- closer to sauteed vegetables than a curry. It pairs well with dal and flatbread.
